projects.name: Enhancing early warning systems by using genomic surveillance and One Health approach in Georgia
projects.description:
The proposed project intends to address the key pandemic prevention, preparedness, and response
(PPR) challenges identified by the JEE 2019 and the 2019 ECDC review, using the One Health
approach to enhance national PPR and strengthen Georgia’s core capacities under the International
Health Regulations (IHR). The project will target gaps identified in the surveillance and the
national laboratory systems and improve regional and local surveillance capacity for both animal
and human health adhering with the one health approach, addressing geographical inequities. As a
cross cutting intervention, under the project will also be conducted a gender gap assessment to
followed by a gender-sensitive data collection and training, with results shared in workshops,
community engagements, and annual reports.

The project objectives focused on building the early warning system (EWS) and AMR surveillance
systems using the One Health approach is fully aligned with the strategic objectives of the National
Action Plan for One Health System Development 2023-2025 and National AMR Strategy
2024-2030 and National AMR Action Plan 2024-2026. The gaps described above will be addressed
by monitoring threats through community and event-based surveillance (EBS) and EWS that
collect, assess, and report potential risks occurring in agricultural settings; implementing sentinel based
surveillance (including for novel influenza strains and AMR) selected industrial and
backyard farms located in vulnerable communities in Georgia; and conducting activities in close
multisectoral collaboration under a unified One Health approach for data collection from farm
animals and poultry, farmers, and the surrounding environment and communities.

1/ To strengthen national capacities in the target countries for the development of comprehensive digital governance policies to better plan and manage integrated power systems for an inclusive and gender-responsive sustainable digital transformation of the energy sector. 
The project is grounded in the understanding that many countries with special needs face fragmented governance systems, outdated and/or damaged infrastructure, and limited technical capacity to integrate digital technologies into power systems. Without structured and inclusive policy frameworks, efforts to deploy smart grids and decentralized renewable energy technologies often remain ad hoc, vulnerable to rebound effects, and unable to ensure interoperability with legacy systems. Additionally, the digital divide, cybersecurity risks, and underrepresentation of women and marginalized groups in energy decision-making processes further hinder the inclusiveness and sustainability of the energy transition.

These frameworks will be complemented by capacity-building workshops (OP1.2) and the creation of a harmonized policy toolkit (OP1.3), helping policymakers and regulators apply digital governance principles in planning, managing, and regulating smart grid systems. 
In parallel, the project will facilitate increased cross-country cooperation through the establishment of a regional platform for knowledge exchange on digital energy governance (OP2.1). This platform will foster peer learning, mentorship, and the sharing of best practices among national institutions, regional actors, and the private sector. Policy briefs and country case studies (OP2.2) will summarize key insights and inform ongoing reforms, while national training events (OP2.3) will reinforce technical capacity and promote a responsible and inclusive digital transition.

2/ To enhance energy system resilience through regional cooperation and energy connectivity. Supporting increased energy security and resilience through energy transition. framework.name: PROMOTING GREEN AND INCLUSIVE DEVELOPMENT TO REDUCE RURAL-URBAN DIVIDE
framework.description:
The overall theory of change for Georgia’s progress towards the SDGs is premised on the interconnectedness of the main components of the 2030 Agenda for sustainable development, and more specifically People, Prosperity, Planet, Partnership, and Peace. Recognizing that sustainable economic growth is inseparable from environmental protection and climate action, this Framework positions these priorities as a unified and essential pillar of its theory of change. It embraces green growth not only as a necessity but as a powerful opportunity to create decent work and sustainable livelihoods. 
Neither the economy nor the planet can truly thrive if the people who inhabit it are unable to realize their full potential throughout their lives. In the context of Georgia, this means ensuring that all people, wherever they live, can expand their learning outcomes, live healthier lives and be supported by a comprehensive social protection system. Lifelong learning opportunities will also ensure that people, especially youth and older people, have the skills required by an evolving labour market, supporting economic development and inclusion. 
To reduce the urban-rural divide and support Georgia in its efforts to maintain peace and foster social cohesion, the change pathway includes furthering decentralization to make service delivery more efficient and well-targeted at the local level and bring the decision-making closer to the people; enhancing access to effective justice and remedies to ensure that all individuals receive legal support and fair treatment; and strengthening the rule of law and reducing social tensions. Establishing strong human rights institutions that operate with transparency and accountability is also considered essential to safeguard freedoms and enforce protections, thus leading to greater social cohesion. Likewise, strengthening legal tools and promoting behavioural change for gender equality will enable greater women’s participation in public life. Expanding the civic space and fostering participatory systems would allow for more meaningful public engagement, leading to more efficient, accountable decision-making and a sense of shared responsibility that can catalyse progress, promote inclusion and reduce social divides.
Georgia’s journey toward a sustainable, peaceful and resilient future hinges on fostering trust between communities divided by conflict and on ensuring access to essential services, viable livelihoods, and the full protection of human rights to all conflict-affected people.

This Outcome reflects a holistic development vision that integrates inclusive economic growth and environmental sustainability. It acknowledges that in Georgia people in rural areas require targeted support as they currently have fewer pathways to benefit from economic opportunities and are more immediately affected by environmental degradation and climate change. It also implies placing low-emission and climate-resilient agriculture at the centre of rural development and integrated value chain development, including in non-agricultural sectors. Other important structural challenges addressed by this Outcome include the relatively large share of workers in the informal sector, the low participation of women in the labour market, and the high proportion of youth not in employment, education or training.

These interventions are designed to reduce disparities, particularly in rural areas, and to align education more closely with labour market needs. A more inclusive education system that can respond to the needs of children with disabilities and other marginalized groups is foundational to breaking cycles of poverty and exclusion.

children.name: 2.2. Capacities of institutions and service providers are enhanced to deliver inclusive quality health and social services, address key health risks, promote well-being, and reach the most vulnerable.
children.description: UN will work to enhance the capacities of institutions and service providers to deliver inclusive, quality health and social services by strengthening universal health coverage, primary health care and continue medical education systems, improving mental health support, promoting healthy lifestyles, and reaching underserved communities through innovative approaches, such as telemedicine and other digital innovative products. These efforts are based on the understanding that health outcomes are shaped by several factors, including behavioural and environmental ones. Promoting well-being requires coordinated action across sectors and sustained investment in both infrastructure and human resources.

children.name: 2.3. The social protection system has improved capacities to identify and respond to population needs and socio-economic changes, including unexpected shocks, thereby reducing life-cycle vulnerabilities for all.
children.description: UN will support the development of a social protection system that can identify and respond to population needs and socio-economic changes, including unexpected shocks. This system must be capable of reaching all individuals—including asylum seekers, refugees, migrants, older persons and people with special needs— at any point throughout their lives. It must also provide protection in the workplace, support survivors of violence, and deliver services effectively at the local level. The implementation of the biopsychosocial model of disability will require additional resources and efforts, but has the potential to transform the lives of people with disabilities. These interventions are critical to reducing life-cycle vulnerabilities and ensuring that social protection is proactive, inclusive and universal.

children.name: OUTCOME 3: GOVERNANCE, HUMAN RIGHTS, GENDER EQUALITY AND SOCIAL COHESION
children.description:
OUTCOME 3: BY 2030, PEOPLE IN GEORGIA BENEFIT FROM A MORE DECENTRALIZED AND INCLUSIVE GOVERNANCE SYSTEM, WITH STRONGER HUMAN RIGHTS PROTECTIONS, GENDER EQUALITY, AND ENHANCED SOCIAL COHESION.
This Outcome envisions a society where governance is not only more decentralized but also more inclusive, participatory and rights-based. Achieving this requires both stronger national and local institutions that are more capable, accountable, and responsive, as well as support to the people of Georgia in becoming more empowered, informed, and engaged.

children.name: 3.1. National and local institutions have enhanced capacities for promoting human rights, gender equality, an inclusive and accessible justice system in line with international commitments, and for fostering inclusive governance and effective decentralization.
children.description:
UN will work to enhance the capacities of national and local institutions to promote human rights, gender equality, and an inclusive and accessible justice system. This includes supporting the alignment of national frameworks with the country’s international human rights commitments. 
Georgia signed and ratified most of the core UN human rights conventions. The UN system will assist the Government of Georgia in meeting its international human rights obligations and commitments, which lie at the heart of sustainable development. 
At the national level, the term ‘gender equality’ was removed from all Georgian laws and replaced by ‘equality between women and men’ in April 2025. Georgia’s international commitments on the rights of all women and girls include Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW, ratified by Georgia in 1994) and its General Recommendations, Council of Europe Convention on Preventing and Combating Violence against Women and Domestic Violence (Istanbul Convention, ratified by Georgia in 2017), Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, outcome documents of the Commission of the Status of Women, and the SDGs, especially Goal 5, which calls for achieving gender equality and empowering all women and girls. 
The UN will work to strengthen the capacity of key institutions to uphold human rights and will facilitate multi-stakeholder dialogues and partnerships on human rights issues. To do so, the UN’s support will be framed by the recommendations of the human rights mechanisms available to Georgia, in particular as a result of the upcoming 4th cycle of the Universal Periodic Review (UPR) in 2026. National priorities in the area of human rights protection were outlined in the National Strategy for the Protection of Human Rights in Georgia 2022-2030, and related action plans, which will continue to inform UN’s support to Georgia. 
Furthermore, by equipping institutions with the competencies and policy tools they need, the UN will contribute to a governance environment that is more transparent, accountable, and inclusive. Leveraging the UN’s strong programmatic experience, such efforts can contribute to strengthening inclusion and sustainability of development progress at the local level.

children.name: 3.2. Civic space, intra-societal dialogue and social cohesion are strengthened.
children.description:
UN will foster civic space, intra-societal dialogue, and social cohesion. This involves building the capacities of civic actors, raising public awareness, and promoting the inclusion of voices that are often marginalized. By building a culture of participation and dialogue, the UN aims to ensure that governance reflects the diversity of Georgia’s society and that all people effectively participate in decision-making processes affecting their lives. 
The rationale behind these interventions is grounded in the evidence that inclusive governance leads to more stable and peaceful societies. When people feel heard and represented, trust in institutions grows, and social cohesion is strengthened. Gender equality and human rights protections are not only moral imperatives but also essential for sustainable development. Decentralization, when effectively implemented, brings decision-making closer to communities and improves service delivery, thereby building trust between government and its citizens.

children.name: OUTCOME 4: AN ENABLING ENVIRONMENT FOR PEACE
children.description:
OUTCOME 4: BY 2030, PEOPLE AFFECTED BY CONFLICT, INCLUDING IDPS, ENJOY ENHANCED ENGAGEMENT, TRUST, AND RESILIENCE FOR AN ENABLING ENVIRONMENT FOR PEACE, ACROSS DIVIDING LINES
This outcome addresses the legacy of unresolved conflict and the resulting social fragmentation, displacement and marginalization on the ground. It highlights the importance of a concerted effort to support populations affected by conflict to ensure that no one is left behind and improve enabling environment of lasting peace. No geographic distinction is made regarding conflict-affected communities, and the term encompasses people in all of Georgia, on either side of the dividing line, including IDPs (with or without official status), and particularly communities adjacent to the dividing line.

children.name: 4.1. Space expanded for inclusive dialogue and confidence-building between divided communities, and for the inclusion of women and youth in promoting peace and security.
children.description: UN will work to expand space for inclusive dialogue and confidence-building between divided communities. This includes creating platforms for engagement and people-to-people contacts, supporting community-led initiatives, and ensuring that women and youth are actively involved in peace and security efforts. These interventions are designed to foster mutual understanding, reduce tensions, and build the social capital necessary for peace.

children.name: 4.2. Conflict-affected people have improved access to essential services, livelihoods and strengthened protection of human rights.
children.description: UN will support conflict-affected people on both sides of the dividing line by improving their access to essential services, livelihoods, and protection of human rights to support the conflict-affected populations in shaping their future in an empowered and dignified way.
